title: The Yips, the Routine, and the Read: Why Putting Decides Golf Championships
summary: Golfers can hit drives 320 yards and iron shots to within feet of the flag, and still lose tournaments on the green. Putting is the most mentally exposed part of golf — and the most decisive.
content:
Golf's cruelest paradox is that its simplest-looking shot is its most decisive. A putt travels a few feet along the ground. No wind resistance, no need for massive power, no technical complexity of the kind that makes a full swing so demanding. And yet putting accounts for approximately 40 percent of all strokes in a professional round, and the difference between winning and losing a golf tournament almost always comes down to what happens on the greens.

The professional golfers who have dominated the game — Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, Ben Crenshaw — were without exception excellent putters. The tour is populated with long hitters who cannot win because their putting abandons them under pressure. The short game, and putting in particular, is where the nervous system expresses itself most nakedly, and where mental composure matters more than anywhere else in the sport.

Reading the Green

Before the stroke itself, the putt must be read. Reading a green — assessing the slope, grain, speed, and break of a putt — is an interpretive skill that develops over years. Two players can stand over the same putt and read it differently. One is right and one is wrong, and they will not know which until the ball has rolled.

The factors that determine how a putt breaks are numerous and interact in complex ways. The slope of the green is the most obvious, but grain — the direction in which the grass grows — creates subtle effects that experienced players learn to read from the colour and texture of the surface. Moisture affects speed. The hardness of the green affects how much the ball slides versus rolls. Elevation changes alter the speed requirement. A thirty-foot putt on a double-breaking green, downhill, on a fast surface, is an exercise in applied geometry that the best putters perform with intuition developed over thousands of hours of practice.

The Stroke Mechanics

Putting strokes vary more than any other aspect of golf. Players use different grips — conventional, cross-handed, the claw — different stances, different stroke paths. What they share, the elite putters, is consistency. The stroke that works under low pressure must work under high pressure. It must repeat. The mechanics that produce a good putt at the practice green must produce the same putt on the 72nd hole of a major championship with a one-shot lead.

This repeatability is why putting grips and techniques evolve over careers. Players who develop inconsistencies — who find that their conventional grip becomes unreliable under pressure — experiment with alternatives that give the nervous system less opportunity to intervene. The cross-handed grip, in which the lower hand and arm are switched to reduce the dominant hand's influence, has helped players who found their dominant hand taking over at crucial moments, flipping the putter head and missing right.

When I am putting well, I am not thinking about mechanics. I see the line, I commit to the line, and I roll the ball. When I am putting badly, there are too many thoughts. The mechanics, the outcome, the consequences. The more you think over a putt, the harder it becomes. The best putting is almost thoughtless.

The Yips

The yips — an involuntary twitch or jerk during the putting stroke — represent golf's most feared psychological condition. Players who develop them describe the sensation of the putter moving independently of their intention, of watching their hands do something they did not instruct them to do, of the stroke they have been making reliably for decades suddenly becoming unreliable in the most important moments.

The yips have ended careers. Bernhard Langer, one of the best players of the 1980s, suffered the yips multiple times and rebuilt his putting technique from scratch on each occasion. Ben Hogan, perhaps the greatest ball striker in history, became so afflicted on the greens in the later part of his career that he effectively could not compete. The yips reveal the extent to which putting is a psychological act as much as a mechanical one.

The Routine as Protection

Every great putter has a routine — a fixed sequence of actions performed before every putt, regardless of the pressure of the situation. The routine is not superstition. It is a psychological anchor. By going through the same actions in the same order, the player activates the same mental state that the routine has become associated with. The routine normalises the moment, making the most pressurised putt feel — at least for the seconds of its execution — like every other putt they have ever hit.

Tiger Woods at his peak had a putting routine so consistent that frame-by-frame comparisons of his pre-putt preparations across different tournaments showed identical timing, identical movements, identical tempo. The routine was the same whether he was putting to win a major or putting on the practice green before the round. That consistency was protective — it meant the pressure could not change his preparation, which meant it was less likely to change his execution.
